title: How Charles Darwin Worked
summary: Josh and Chuck profile Charles Darwin the man: his upbringing and medical-school detour, the voyage of the HMS Beagle under Robert FitzRoy, the Galapagos, his years at Down House studying nature and raising a family, his procrastination over natural selection, the competing work of Alfred Russell Wallace, the publication of On the Origin of Species in 1859, the backlash and supporters such as Thomas Huxley, and how Darwin's ideas were later twisted into social Darwinism and eugenics. The episode closes with a listener letter from an amputee and a reading of the Origin's closing paragraph.

segments.title: Opening banter and evolution debate
segments.summary: The hosts open with casual banter, then discuss evolution and natural selection, the Bill Nye versus Ken Ham debate, and the aim of the episode not to attack anyone's beliefs.

segments.title: Darwin's early life and education
segments.summary: Darwin's father wanted him to be a doctor, but he disliked surgery and turned to natural science. He studied at Shrewsbury, Edinburgh and Christ's College, Cambridge, and his father then pushed him toward becoming a country parson. He was agnostic from an early age.

segments.title: Joining the HMS Beagle
segments.summary: At age 21 Darwin accepted Robert FitzRoy's invitation to join the five-year HMS Beagle survey voyage around South America. He spent much of the voyage on land collecting specimens.

segments.title: Galapagos and the return to England
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the Galapagos, where Darwin spent about five weeks, and say its significance was overstated. Darwin's specimens and papers made him a celebrity on his return. His notebooks were first titled the Transmutation Notebooks.

segments.title: Malthus and the origins of natural selection
segments.summary: Darwin and Alfred Russell Wallace were both inspired by Thomas Malthus's Essay on the Principle of Population, which argued that scarcity and competition drive change. Darwin's life at Down House, his family, his experiments with earthworms, orchids and pigeons, and his Sandwalk are described.
topics: Essay on the Principle of Population

segments.title: Darwin's family, marriage and health
segments.summary: Darwin married his first cousin Emma Wedgwood, who cared for him through his chronic illness. They had ten children, three of whom died. Darwin worried about inbreeding and his children's deaths, and his wife was concerned about their afterlife.

segments.title: Procrastination, the Vestiges, and Wallace's letter
segments.summary: Darwin delayed publishing out of care and fear of backlash. The anonymous Vestiges of the Natural History of Creation prompted him to revise his work. Wallace's letter with a similar theory led to a joint presentation at the Linnean Society and then Darwin's publication in 1859.
topics: Vestiges of the Natural History of Creation

segments.title: Creationism, catastrophism and the Origin of Species
segments.summary: The hosts explain the prevailing creationist view, Cuvier's catastrophism for fossils, and the core argument of On the Origin of Species about variation, competition and survival. Darwin avoided stating human descent outright, though the implication was clear to Victorians.

segments.title: Reaction, Wallace's standing, and Huxley
segments.summary: Darwin's work drew backlash and cartoons but also supporters. Wallace was overlooked partly because he sold specimens and lacked Darwin's social standing. Thomas Huxley became Darwin's defender, known as Darwin's bulldog, and is credited with coining the term agnostic.

segments.title: Legacy, social Darwinism and eugenics
segments.summary: Herbert Spencer applied Darwinism to society as social Darwinism, which fed the eugenics movement and was used by the Nazis. US states forced sterilizations. The hosts dispute the deathbed recantation story, which was denied by Darwin's children, and argue that ancient remains show human compassion for the disabled.

segments.title: Listener mail: amputee and a closing reading
segments.summary: A listener who had a leg amputated corrects an earlier comment, describing her life and prosthetics. The hosts read the closing paragraph of On the Origin of Species, then sign off with ways to contact the show.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts close the episode, mention related Darwin resources, and invite listeners to share stories and get in touch.
